newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hardline policies risk Israel's peace dividend.
newsitem.headline: Hardline policies risk Israel's peace dividend.

text.p: The Israeli economy reaped great rewards from the peace accord with the PLO in 1993 but investors are warning those rewards are at risk from the policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Israel is at a critical junction and it has to figure out which way to go -- one way is Japan, the other is Bosnia," said Jonathan Kolber, head of Claridge Israel, the Israeli investment vehicle for Charles Bronfman of Canada.
Israel currently seems to be heading in the direction of Bosnia, Kolber added.
Netanyahu's decision last week to open a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem unleashed violent demonstrations and gun fights that killed 55 Palestinians and 14 Israelis.
The Tel Aviv stock market dropped over six percent in reaction. The shekel has fallen against the dollar and foreign investors remain sidelined.

Arab countries have been rethinking normalisation of relations with the Jewish state, begun under the previous government. Qatar warned it was considering putting further ties with Israel on hold and Morocco's opposition called on Arab states to freeze relations with Israel.

Yoram Gabbay, head of one of Bank Hapoalim's investment- management companies, said that as a result of the peace accord Israel's exports have doubled, foreign investment has grown to $2 billion a year against $500 million before and foreign investments in real assets reached $870 million, against almost none before.

Foreign investors poured money into Israel and tourism boomed. Previously-closed markets in Asia and the Middle East opened up to the Jewish state, and Israeli and Arab businessmen began making deals.

"A continuation of the peace process is very important to Israel as well as Jordan and the surrounding countries. A slowing of the peace process may slow inward investment by international investors," said Stephen Marquardt, managing director of investment banking at Merrill Lynch.

Since May 29 elections in which Netanyahu toppled Nobel Peace Prize winner Shimon Peres and his Labour party from government, business relations between Israel and Arab states have cooled as progress in the peace talks came to a halt.
"Since the elections it's no secret that interest, interaction between the sides has fallen," said Doron Peskin head of research at Info-Prod Research, specialising in Middle East markets.
Foreigners have also been less eager to invest in Israel.

"At present we aren't too enthusiastic about putting money into the economy," said Kolber. He blamed the three months of stagnation in the peace process, since Netanyahu came to power, for the political tensions.

This investment is vital to Israel as the new government grapples with economic problems inherited from Labour -- widening deficits in the budget and balance of payments current account as well as rising inflation.
The political crisis is likely to distract the government's attention from resolving these pressing economic issues, said Eran Goren, managing director of Zannex Securities.
"When the country is on fire, the government can't deal with issues such as the budget," he said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has invited Middle East leaders to an emergency summit in Washington this week to try and resolve the crisis.
Peskin was optimistic a solution would be found, saying it was unlikely Clinton would risk a summit just five weeks before U.S. elections unless he had some sort of prior commitment from both sides.
"If there is going to be a summit the results will be there. But it will not take a short time to rebuild confidence," he said. Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211
